title: Differential testing: what it establishes
objective: Predict from a generator's statistics alone whether a differential suite detects a planted bug, then stamp a passing run with its full qualifier.

blocks.md: Your compiler runs. The next question is what a test of it can tell you. A differential suite feeds the same generated commands to a reference and to the compiled plan on a real database, then compares outcome classes: committed, refused for a named reason, or an error code.

choice.prompt: A suite ran n generated transfers through the reference interpreter and the compiled plan on a database, and found no divergence. Which stamp fits?

options.why: Many passing runs are still runs.
No bounded space was explored exhaustively.
Nothing checks production at run time.
The qualifier says how many commands were run and what kind.

blocks.md: The cell below is a small harness in SQL. Its reference is a rule standing in for the course's interpreter: it rejects a self-transfer, refuses an overdraft and commits everything else. The plan under test is the one-statement CASE compile from S6.L2. The generator draws accounts 1 to 3 with `from` and `to` different, and amounts 1 to 200.

blocks.direction: Each `suite(n, self_pct)` call runs n commands, with `self_pct` percent of them self-transfers, and prints its statistics and its first divergence, if any. Edit the numbers and run again.

call.prompt: Before you run it: will `suite(300, 0)` report a divergence from the CASE plan within its commands?

options.text: Yes, within a few hundred commands.
options.why: The generator never draws `from = to`, so the bug is unreachable however many commands run.
Its statistics line shows no self-transfers. A test finds only what its generator reaches.
Nothing in the plan stops execution.

blocks.after: The default generator found nothing, and its statistics line says why. With a 5 percent self-transfer quota the first divergence appears, with its command number and both outcome classes. {{run:RUN-drt-transfers}}

blocks.md: A passing run earns `TESTED [T]` with its qualifier: how many commands ran, and the generator's statistics, meaning each outcome class's share, the self-transfer share and the largest balance reached. The last one returns in S6.L4. Engines belong in the stamp too. PGlite reports PostgreSQL 18.6 {{run:RUN-pglite-0511}}, so agreement on PGlite and on a Bench server is one semantics checked twice. The claim below keeps that assumption visible as a seam, drawn dashed: one database's agreement stands for the compiler. A later stage tests it.

choice.prompt: A receipt for a differential run shows 300 commands, no divergence, PGlite and a Bench server both named, the share of each outcome class, a self-transfer share of 0 percent, and the largest balance reached. Which line stamps it?

options.why: A run is not a proof, however clean.
A count with no statistics hides what the generator never reached.

options.text: `TESTED [T] · 300 commands · class shares and self-transfer share · both engines named`
options.why: The qualifier carries the count, what the generator drew and where it ran.
Both engines report one server code base, so agreement is one check, not two.

options.text: A class of command the generator never draws is untested.
options.why: The suite can only diverge on commands it runs.

options.text: The compiled plan matches the interpreter on every possible command.
options.why: A run covers the commands it drew, and nothing more.

options.text: PGlite and a real server agreeing is two independent checks.
options.why: They share one code base, so a common-mode bug passes both.

options.text: Comparing final balances alone would catch a plan that overdrafts through the CHECK.
options.why: Balances can match while the outcome differs, as the CHECK-only plan shows.

blocks.title: Production twin: Cedar
blocks.md: Cedar compares its production implementation with its formal model on randomly generated inputs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01688, section 4, read 2026-10-23; pins in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}). Section 4.3 notes that full line coverage still sent many inputs only through error handling. What does Cedar compare, and where would you read its generator's statistics?

blocks.title: Build this
blocks.md: Next, write your own generator and comparison. Choose the classes you draw, set quotas for the rare ones, and read the statistics panel. The course's mutants test your suite.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Disselkoen et al., "How We Built Cedar" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01688), section 4, read 2026-10-23.

notes: First-load sizes are what the engine requested on a cold load of a page whose module worker imports PGlite and makes one query; the page and worker files are excluded. Wire sizes are gzip bodies made on the host with stock zlib at level 5, the level at which GitHub Pages' gzip output matched byte for byte on four probed public files; GitHub Pages sent gzip and no Brotli to a client that offered both.

No `.data` file was probed and no file as large as pglite.wasm was probed (the probed files are under 1 MB), so the host's behavior for a 10 MB wasm file is an assumption until the first deployment is measured. Brotli sizes are what a host that encoded with Brotli 11 would send; GitHub Pages does not.

Browser timings are desktop engines on a 20-CPU host, not phones. Chromium's CPU throttle does not reach a worker (the probe loop does not slow), so the slow-CPU configurations cap the whole container's CPU quota instead: an emulation that slows every browser thread together, pessimistic for a multi-core phone, calibrated by the probe loop. Neither is a phone measurement.

wasm_memory_bytes is the byte length of the instance's linear memory, read from the Emscripten module; resident memory is the sum of VmRSS of every process in the container except the driver, sampled every 100 ms.
The load average at the start and end is in the environment block; other work ran on the machine at the same time, so timings are indicative, not benchmark-grade.
RUN-pglite's scripts ran unchanged on 0.5.11 and on 0.5.10; pglite_check.mjs ran on 0.5.11 only, because it resolves the package by its name.
RUN-pglite-rls and RUN-pglite-0511 come from one invocation of run-all.mjs; each lists the commands it used under configs and setup.
